subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Year 7! This unit opens the door to a bigger world of numbers than the one you have used so far. Until now, almost every number you counted with was a positive whole number: the goats coming home at dusk, the shillings in your pocket at the Hargeisa market, the pages left in a book. Positive numbers are perfect for counting things you can hold. But the real world also contains ideas that go below zero – a temperature five degrees below freezing, a bank account overdrawn by twenty dollars, a diver forty metres beneath the surface of the sea near Berbera. To describe these, you need integers.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Estimate, multiply and divide integers including where one integer is negative.
Understand lowest common multiple and highest common factor (numbers less than 100).
Use knowledge of tests of divisibility to find factors of numbers greater than 100.
Understand the relationship between squares and corresponding square roots, and cubes and corresponding cube roots.
Estimate, add and subtract integers, recognising generalisations.
Estimate, add and subtract positive and negative numbers with the same or different number of decimal places.

outcomes: Understand that integers include positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers, and zero, and place them correctly on a number line.
Compare and order integers, and explain why -10 is less than -5 even though 10 is greater than 5.
Find the opposite of an integer and the absolute value of an integer.
Add and subtract integers using the number line and the sign rules, including subtracting a negative.
Multiply and divide integers using the sign rules, and explain *why* a negative times a negative is positive.
Find multiples and the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers.
Find factors and the highest common factor (HCF) of two or more numbers.
Calculate square roots and cube roots of perfect squares and cubes, and estimate other roots.
Use the correct order of operations with powers, roots and integers, and solve real-world problems.

concepts.title: Integers and the Number Line
concepts.explanation:
The number line is your most powerful tool for understanding integers. Picture a straight horizontal line stretching forever in both directions, with zero at the centre. To the right of zero sit the positive integers (1, 2, 3, 4, …). To the left of zero sit the negative integers (-1, -2, -3, -4, …). Every integer has exactly one home on this line.

The number line makes the order of integers obvious. As you move from left to right, numbers always increase. As you move from right to left, they decrease. This single idea clears up the most common confusion about negative numbers. Many learners think -10 must be bigger than -5 because 10 is bigger than 5. But on the line, -10 sits further to the left than -5, so -10 is less than -5. Think of temperature: -10°C is colder than -5°C, and colder means lower, means less. We write this as -10 < -5.

The number line also shows opposites. Every positive integer has a matching negative integer the same distance from zero but on the other side. For example, 3 and -3 are opposites because both are exactly 3 units from zero. Zero is special: it is its own opposite. Finding an opposite simply flips the sign, so the opposite of -8 is 8, and the opposite of 15 is -15. Watch out for the double negative: the opposite of -8 is 8, which we can write as -(-8) = 8. A minus sign in front of a negative number flips it back to positive.

Next comes absolute value, which means the distance of a number from zero, ignoring its direction. Distance is never negative, so absolute value is never negative. Both 4 and -4 have an absolute value of 4, because both are 4 units from zero. We write it with vertical bars: |4| = 4 and |-4| = 4. Do not confuse absolute value with 'make it positive by force' – the idea is really about distance. If you stand at position -3 on the line and walk to position 2, you travel a distance of 5 units, even though you started on a negative number and ended on a positive one.
concepts.example: Let us put these ideas together with a real example. Suppose the floors of a tall building in Nairobi are numbered so that the ground floor is 0, floors above are positive, and the underground car-park levels are negative. Yusuf parks on level -3 and rides the lift up to floor 5. To compare the two positions we note that -3 < 5, and to find how far he travelled we count the units between them: from -3 up to 0 is 3 units, then from 0 up to 5 is 5 more, giving 8 units in all. Reading positions, ordering them, and measuring distances between them are exactly the skills the number line gives you.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Integers
concepts.explanation: Adding and subtracting integers can feel tricky at first, but two clear methods will carry you through every problem: the number-line method and the sign rules. Learn both, because each helps you understand the other. When two integers have the same sign, add their absolute values and keep the shared sign. If both are positive, this is ordinary addition: 5 + 3 = 8. If both are negative, add the sizes and keep the minus: (-5) + (-3) = -8. Think of debt: if Hassan owes 5 shillings and then borrows another 3, he owes 8 shillings in total.
concepts.example: When the signs are different, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger, and keep the sign of the number with the larger absolute value. For 7 + (-3), the sizes are 7 and 3; subtract to get 4, and since 7 is larger and positive, the answer is +4. For (-7) + 3, the sizes are still 7 and 3, the difference is 4, but this time the larger size belongs to -7, so the answer is -4. On the number line, adding a positive means moving right and adding a negative means moving left. To work out (-2) + 5, start at -2 and move 5 steps right, landing on 3.

concepts.title: Multiplying and Dividing Integers
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying and dividing integers follow one neat pattern about signs, plus a good reason why the pattern is true. Once you understand it, these operations become the easiest part of the unit.

The sign rules are short: same signs give a positive result, different signs give a negative result. For multiplication that means positive × positive = positive (3 × 4 = 12), negative × negative = positive ((-3) × (-4) = 12), positive × negative = negative (3 × (-4) = -12), and negative × positive = negative ((-3) × 4 = -12). Division follows exactly the same rules, because division is just multiplication in reverse: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, (-12) ÷ (-3) = 4, 12 ÷ (-3) = -4, and (-12) ÷ 3 = -4.

But why does a negative times a negative make a positive? Memorising a rule is not the same as understanding it. Think of multiplication as repeated addition. 3 × 4 means 'add 4, three times': 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Now 3 × (-4) means 'add -4, three times': (-4) + (-4) + (-4) = -12. So far so good. What about (-3) × (-4)? The negative in front of the 3 means 'do the opposite'. The opposite of adding -4 three times (which loses you 12) is gaining 12. In real language: removing a debt is the same as gaining money. If someone cancels three debts of 4 shillings each, you are 12 shillings better off, so (-3) × (-4) = +12. The rule is not arbitrary; it keeps the whole number system consistent.

A helpful shortcut for longer products is to count the negative signs. If there is an even number of negative factors, the product is positive; if there is an odd number, the product is negative. For example, (-2) × (-3) × (-1) has three negative signs – an odd number – so the product is negative: first (-2) × (-3) = 6, then 6 × (-1) = -6. Meanwhile (-7) × (+4) × (-2) has two negatives – an even number – so the product is positive: (-7) × 4 = -28, then -28 × (-2) = 56.
concepts.example: These operations appear everywhere in science and business. In physics, velocity can be positive or negative depending on direction, and multiplying a negative velocity by a time gives a negative displacement (movement backwards). In business, if a shop loses 3 shillings on each of 40 items sold at a loss, the total change is 40 × (-3) = -120 shillings. Learning to attach the correct sign to each quantity, then following the sign rules, lets you solve these problems with confidence.

concepts.title: Multiples and the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM)
concepts.explanation:
A multiple of a number is what you get when you multiply that number by an integer. The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, … found by multiplying 6 by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and so on. Because you can always multiply by a larger integer, the list of multiples of any number goes on forever.

The lowest common multiple, or LCM, of two or more numbers is the smallest positive number that is a multiple of all of them. The LCM is the tool you use to add or subtract fractions with different denominators, because it gives the lowest common denominator. There are two main methods for finding it.

The listing method works well for small numbers. Write out the multiples of each number until you find the smallest one they share. To find the LCM of 4 and 6: the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, … and the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, … The first number that appears in both lists is 12, so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.

The prime factorisation method is faster and more reliable for larger numbers. First write each number as a product of prime factors. Then, for the LCM, take each prime the greatest number of times it appears in any one number, and multiply. For 12 and 18: 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3². The greatest power of 2 present is 2², and the greatest power of 3 present is 3², so the LCM is 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36. This works because the LCM must contain enough of each prime to be divisible by every original number.
concepts.example: LCM solves real scheduling puzzles. Suppose one bus to Mombasa leaves every 15 minutes and another every 20 minutes, and both leave together at 8:00 a.m. They will next leave together after LCM(15, 20) minutes. Since 15 = 3 × 5 and 20 = 2² × 5, the LCM is 2² × 3 × 5 = 60 minutes, so they coincide again at 9:00 a.m. The same reasoning explains when two bells ring together, when gears line up, or when repeating events fall on the same day.

concepts.title: Factors and the Highest Common Factor (HCF)
concepts.explanation:
A factor of a number is any integer that divides into it exactly, with no remainder. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, because each of these divides 12 evenly. Factors are always less than or equal to the number itself, and every number has 1 and itself as factors.

The highest common factor, or HCF (also called the greatest common divisor), is the largest integer that divides two or more numbers exactly. It is the tool you use to simplify fractions and to split quantities into the largest equal groups. Again there are two dependable methods.

The listing method: write all the factors of each number and pick the largest they share. For 18 and 24, the factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18 and the factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, and the highest of these is 6, so HCF(18, 24) = 6.

The prime factorisation method: write each number as a product of primes, then multiply together the primes they share, using the lowest power of each. For 60 and 84: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. Both share 2² and 3, so the HCF is 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12. Notice the contrast with LCM: for the HCF you take shared primes at the lowest power, while for the LCM you take all primes at the highest power. Keeping this difference straight prevents the most common mix-up in the whole unit.
concepts.example: The HCF has satisfying real uses. To simplify the fraction 18/24, divide the top and bottom by their HCF of 6 to get 3/4 – fully simplified in one step. In sharing problems, the HCF tells you the largest equal group possible: if Amina has 144 dates and 108 sambusas to arrange into identical gift trays with nothing left over, the largest number of trays is HCF(144, 108). Since 144 = 2⁴ × 3² and 108 = 2² × 3³, the HCF is 2² × 3² = 36 trays.

concepts.title: Tests for Divisibility
concepts.explanation:
Divisibility tests are shortcuts that tell you whether one number divides exactly into another, without doing the full division. They save time when finding factors, simplifying fractions, and building prime factorisations. Here are the tests you need for this unit.

Divisible by 2: the number ends in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6 or 8).

Divisible by 3: the sum of the digits is divisible by 3. For 2,847 the digits sum to 2+8+4+7 = 21, and 21 is divisible by 3, so 2,847 is too.

Divisible by 4: the number formed by the last two digits is divisible by 4. For 3,716 the last two digits are 16, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so 3,716 is divisible by 4.

Divisible by 5: the number ends in 0 or 5.

Divisible by 6: the number is divisible by both 2 and 3 (because 6 = 2 × 3).

Divisible by 8: the number formed by the last three digits is divisible by 8. For 5,624 the last three digits are 624, and 624 ÷ 8 = 78, so it passes.

Divisible by 9: the sum of the digits is divisible by 9. For 4,536 the digits sum to 18, which is divisible by 9.

Divisible by 10: the number ends in 0.
concepts.example: These tests become even more powerful when you combine them. To test divisibility by 12, check divisibility by both 3 and 4, because 12 = 3 × 4 and 3 and 4 share no common factor. To test divisibility by 15, check both 3 and 5. Understanding *why* the tests work deepens your grasp of number theory: the tests for 2, 5 and 10 depend on the last digit because our system is base 10; the tests for 3 and 9 depend on digit sums because 10 leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 3 or 9. You do not need to prove these in Year 7, but knowing there is a reason – not magic – is part of thinking like a mathematician.

methods.title: How to find the LCM
steps: Write each number as a product of prime factors.
Take every prime that appears, at its highest power in any number.
Multiply these together — that is the LCM.

methods.title: How to find the HCF
steps: Write each number as a product of prime factors.
Take only the primes that are shared, at their lowest power.
Multiply these together — that is the HCF.

methods.title: For a cube root, ask: what number times itself three times gives this value?
steps: If it is not a perfect square or cube, estimate using the nearest perfect ones.
Test numbers close to your estimate by cubing them until you find an exact or close match.
Check by cubing your final answer — it should equal (or nearly equal) the original number.

methods.title: Temperature change
methods.example: At 6 a.m. the temperature was -12°C. It rose 3°C each hour until noon (6 hours), then fell 2°C each hour until 6 p.m. (6 hours). Find the temperature at 6 p.m.
steps: Rise over 6 hours: 6 × 3 = 18, so at noon the temperature is -12 + 18 = 6°C.
Fall over 6 hours: 6 × 2 = 12, so at 6 p.m.

methods.title: LCM by prime factorisation
steps: Take each prime at its highest power: 2², 3 and 5.

methods.title: HCF by prime factorisation
steps: Take only the shared primes at their lowest power: 2² and 3.
The HCF is 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.

workedExamples.title: Order a set of integers
workedExamples.solution: On the number line, the further left, the smaller. The negatives come first, and among negatives a larger size means smaller value, so -12 < -3. Then comes 0, then the positives. The order is -12, -3, 0, +5, +8.

workedExamples.title: Subtract a negative
workedExamples.solution: Subtracting a negative is adding the opposite: (-12) — (-5) = (-12) + (+5). Different signs, so subtract sizes 12 and 5 to get 7, and keep the sign of the larger size (12, negative). The answer is -7.

workedExamples.title: A chain of multiplications
workedExamples.solution: Count the negative signs: there are two, an even number, so the result is positive. Multiply the sizes: 7 × 4 × 2 = 56. The answer is +56. Check by steps: (-7) × 4 = -28, then -28 × (-2) = +56.

workedExamples.title: Temperature change
workedExamples.prompt: At 6 a.m. the temperature was -12°C. It rose 3°C each hour until noon (6 hours), then fell 2°C each hour until 6 p.m. (6 hours). Find the temperature at 6 p.m.
workedExamples.solution: Rise over 6 hours: 6 × 3 = 18, so at noon the temperature is -12 + 18 = 6°C. Fall over 6 hours: 6 × 2 = 12, so at 6 p.m. it is 6 — 12 = -6°C.

workedExamples.title: LCM by prime factorisation
workedExamples.solution: 15 = 3 × 5 and 20 = 2² × 5. Take each prime at its highest power: 2², 3 and 5. The LCM is 2² × 3 × 5 = 4 × 15 = 60.

workedExamples.title: HCF by prime factorisation
workedExamples.solution: 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². Take only the shared primes at their lowest power: 2² and 3. The HCF is 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.

workedExamples.title: A divisibility check
workedExamples.solution: A number is divisible by 6 if it is divisible by both 2 and 3. It ends in 4, an even digit, so it passes the test for 2. Its digits sum to 7+5+2+4 = 18, which is divisible by 3, so it passes the test for 3. Since it passes both, 7,524 is divisible by 6.

workedExamples.title: Roots and order of operations
workedExamples.solution: Handle the roots first (indices in BIDMAS). √144 = 12 because 12 × 12 = 144, and ∛27 = 3 because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Then add: 12 + 3 = 15.

workedExamples.title: Powers of negative numbers
workedExamples.solution: Indices and root first: (-5)² = 25 (even power, positive), (-2)³ = -8 (odd power, negative), √36 = 6. Then left to right: 25 + (-8) — 6 = 17 — 6 = 11.

workedExamples.title: A tiling problem
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular floor is 144 cm by 108 cm. What is the largest square tile that fits a whole number of times along both sides?
workedExamples.solution: The tile side must divide both 144 and 108, and we want the largest such number — the HCF. 144 = 2⁴ × 3² and 108 = 2² × 3³, so the HCF is 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36 cm. A 36 cm tile fits 4 times along 144 cm and 3 times along 108 cm.

workedExamples.title: Divisibility tests together
workedExamples.prompt: Test 5,624 for divisibility by 8, and test 4,536 for divisibility by 9. Show your reasoning.
workedExamples.solution: 5,624: last three digits 624, and 624 ÷ 8 = 78, so yes. 4,536: digit sum 18, divisible by 9, so yes.

workedExamples.title: Order of operations with powers and roots
workedExamples.prompt: Evaluate (-5)² + (-2)³ — √36 using the order of operations.

activities.title: Build a Human Number Line
activities.materials: chalk or a long strip of paper, and space on the ground.
steps: Mark a line on the ground from -10 to +10 with zero in the middle.
Stand on zero. Call out an integer and step to it – right for positive, left for negative.
Practise addition by walking: to do (-3) + 5, start on -3 and take 5 steps right.
Practise subtraction by turning it into 'add the opposite': for 4 - (-3), start on 4 and step 3 to the right.
Ask a family member (or your AI tutor) to call out sums and race to land on the right answer.

activities.title: Two-Colour Counters (Positive and Negative)
activities.materials: about 30 small objects in two colours – for example light stones for positive and dark stones for negative.
steps: Let each light stone stand for +1 and each dark stone for -1.
A light and a dark stone together make a 'zero pair' and cancel out.
Model (-5) + 3 by laying 5 dark and 3 light stones, removing zero pairs, and reading what is left (-2).
Model 4 + (-6) the same way, and check your answer against the sign rules.
Invent three of your own additions and solve them with the stones.

activities.title: The Integer Card Game
activities.materials: paper cards numbered from -10 to +10 (write them yourself), and a partner such as a family member or your AI tutor (or play both hands yourself if alone).
steps: Shuffle the cards and deal each player one card face down.
Both players flip their cards over at the same time.
The player whose card is greater wins the round – remember -2 beats -7.
For a harder version, each player flips two cards and adds them; the larger sum wins.
Play until the cards run out, then count who won more rounds.

activities.title: LCM and HCF Investigation
activities.materials: paper, pencil, and a set of small objects to group.
steps: Choose two numbers, for example 8 and 12, and write out the first ten multiples of each.
Ring the first multiple they share – that is the LCM.
Now list the factors of each number and ring the largest they share – that is the HCF.
Check the rule: does LCM × HCF equal the two numbers multiplied together?
Repeat with a new pair and see whether the rule holds every time.

activities.title: Perfect Squares and Cubes Hunt
activities.materials: small square tiles or drawn grid paper, and a few small cubes or boxes.
steps: Arrange tiles into squares: 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, and so on. Record the number of tiles each time – these are the perfect squares.
Explain why the side length is the square root of the number of tiles.

Test yourself: cover the chart and write as many as you can from memory.

activities.title: Divisibility Detective (Family Game)
activities.materials: your family, friends, or your AI tutor, and paper to write large numbers.
steps: One person writes a four-digit number in secret.
Others use the divisibility tests to predict which of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 divide it.
The writer checks each prediction with real division.
Score one point for each correct prediction; the detective with the most points wins.
Swap roles and play again with a new number.

rules.title: Ordering Rule
rules.text: On the number line, further right means greater, further left means smaller. Among negatives, a larger size means a smaller value: -10 < -5.

rules.title: Add and Subtract Rule
rules.text: Same signs: add the sizes and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract the sizes and keep the sign of the larger size. Subtracting a number is adding its opposite: 8 - (-3) = 8 + 3 = 11.

rules.title: Multiply and Divide Rule
rules.text: Same signs give a positive result; different signs give a negative result. Count the minus signs: an even number gives positive, an odd number gives negative.

rules.title: Order of Operations Rule (BIDMAS)
rules.text: Order of Operations (BIDMAS) Brackets, then Indices (powers and roots), then Divide and Multiply, then Add and Subtract. Divide and multiply rank equally, left to right; so do add and subtract.

questions.question: A submarine at sea level (0 m) dives to a depth of 35 m below the surface. Which integer represents its position?
questions.hint: Ask yourself what "Integer" means here before you choose.
questions.explanation: Below sea level is represented by a negative integer, so 35 m below the surface is -35.

questions.question: Which of these lists the integers in order from smallest to largest: -8, 2, -3, 0?
questions.hint: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
questions.explanation: On the number line, -8 is furthest left (smallest), then -3, then 0, then 2, so the order is -8, -3, 0, 2.

questions.question: What is |-9| minus the opposite of 4?
questions.hint: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
questions.explanation: |-9| = 9 and the opposite of 4 is -4, so 9 - (-4) = 9 + 4 = 13.

questions.question: Calculate: -8 - (-15)
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding its opposite: -8 - (-15) = -8 + 15 = 7.

questions.question: What is (-6) × (-7) ÷ (-2)?
questions.hint: Ask yourself what "Factor" means here before you choose.
questions.explanation: (-6) × (-7) = 42 because same signs give a positive result. Then 42 ÷ (-2) = -21 because different signs give a negative result.

questions.question: What is the LCM of 9 and 12?
questions.hint: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
questions.explanation: 9 = 3² and 12 = 2² × 3. Taking each prime at its highest power gives 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36.

questions.question: What is the HCF of 42 and 56?
questions.hint: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
questions.explanation: 42 = 2 × 3 × 7 and 56 = 2³ × 7. The shared primes at their lowest power are 2 and 7, so the HCF is 2 × 7 = 14.

I can add and subtract integers using the number line and the sign rules, including subtracting a negative.
I can multiply and divide integers using the sign rules, and explain *why* a negative times a negative is positive.
I can find multiples and the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers.
I can find factors and the highest common factor (HCF) of two or more numbers.
I can apply divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10.
I can calculate square roots and cube roots of perfect squares and cubes, and estimate other roots.
I can use the correct order of operations with powers, roots and integers, and solve real-world problems.
